memory_candidates.content: When measuring whether a prose addition to an eager-loaded context file (anything feeding the assembled CLAUDE.md) fits a tight byte budget, iterate against the live measure-eager-context.sh --check output rather than hand-counting bytes in the draft text -- hand estimates were consistently off by a wide margin (estimated ~250 B recoverable, iterated wording needed several rounds against the tool). The tool's wc -c-based measurement of the actually-assembled document is the only reliable signal; treat prose-length arithmetic as a rough first guess only.

A test fixture that symlinks .claude -> the real repo tree (rather than copying/regenerating it) to get a 'real deployed scripts chain' for cheap will transitively inherit ANY real-tree finding from a full-battery verify-deploy.sh run against that fixture -- including unrelated runtime litter like orphan-detection hits on other sessions' tmp/ files. A failure traced to such a fixture should always be cross-checked against the SAME gate run directly on the real tree before concluding the fixture (or the code under test) is broken; grep the fixture-builder script for 'ln -s' against the real repo root as the first diagnostic step.

Before adding a new header-comment paragraph to a script whose own existing comments deliberately avoid spelling out certain tool/script names (a 'check-only contract' enforced by a sibling test grepping for the literal string, e.g. test-postflight-deploy-gate.sh grepping update-task-status.sh for 'verify-deploy'/'deploy-headless'), grep the target file for its own established euphemism convention (e.g. 'the deploy-verification entry point') and reuse it, rather than writing a natural-sounding enumeration that reintroduces the literal name. This exact mistake was made and caught only by running the full test suite, not by review -- a targeted grep for the forbidden substrings immediately after drafting new prose in such a file would catch it for free.
